Vienna eats two ways at once.

On one side is the imperial table. It has breaded veal, boiled beef from a copper pot, and chocolate cake. The cake comes from a hotel that dates its recipe to 1832. On the other side is the neighbourhood tavern, the sausage stand, and the market stall. Start hungry.

## The dishes that define Vienna

Start with the Wiener Schnitzel, the dish the city is known for. A real Wiener Schnitzel is always veal, a thin cutlet pounded flat, breaded and fried. The crust puffs away from the meat. Austrian labelling rules reserve the name for veal. A pork version must be sold as Schnitzel Wiener Art. At a neighbourhood Beisl, a veal schnitzel typically costs €18–26. At Meissl & Schadn, the veal schnitzel costs €30.90. Figlmüller claims to be the home of the Wiener Schnitzel. Its plate-sized pork schnitzel has been served since 1905. It costs €21.90.

Tafelspitz is the other imperial classic. It is prime beef, simmered slowly in broth with root vegetables. It is served in its broth with roasted potatoes, creamed spinach, and apple horseradish. Emperor Franz Joseph is said to have eaten it daily. Plachutta is the Viennese institution for boiled beef. It lists more than ten cuts. It charges €36.80 for its Tafelspitz.

For something faster, walk to a Würstelstand. It is the sausage stand that stays open after the bars close. The Käsekrainer is a lightly smoked pork sausage with cheese inside, which melts as it grills. It comes sliced with mustard and a slice of bread. Recent listings put a sausage at roughly €5 to €7. Goulash is the other tavern staple. It is beef and onion cooked down with paprika. It is served with a bread roll or a dumpling. A small beef goulash at a cellar tavern costs €14.20. A large one costs €18.40.

Leave room for cake. The Original Sacher-Torte is a dense chocolate sponge with apricot jam under a dark chocolate glaze. A young apprentice first made the cake in 1832 for a visiting Prince Metternich. A slice with cream costs €11.50 at Café Sacher. Apfelstrudel is paper-thin pastry rolled around spiced apple and raisins. Meissl & Schadn sells apple strudel for €8.50. Kaiserschmarrn is a pancake torn into pieces as it cooks. It is caramelised with sugar and served with vanilla sauce. It costs €12.90 a portion.

## Coffee houses: where Vienna slows down

In 2011, Austria added Vienna's coffee-house culture to its national list of cultural heritage. The legend says it began when the Ottoman army left coffee beans behind after the siege of 1683. There are more than 800 coffee houses in Vienna. Order a Melange. It is an espresso under steamed milk and foam. It arrives with a glass of water. A Melange costs about €4.80 to €5.80 in a traditional coffee house. Order one Melange and stay all afternoon. No one will hurry you along. Sausage-stand culture joined the same heritage list in 2024.

## Markets: eat your way through the Naschmarkt

Naschmarkt is Vienna's best-known food market. Its stalls sell spices, cheese, olives, and Levantine food. The stalls open Monday to Saturday. The market is closed on Sundays. A Saturday flea market runs beside the Naschmarkt at Kettenbrücke. Smaller markets reward a detour. The Karmelitermarkt in Leopoldstadt is busiest on Saturday. The Brunnenmarkt in Ottakring is one of Europe's longest street markets. Go hungry and mid-morning. Graze on samples. Do your serious eating at the sit-down places behind the stalls.

## Wine taverns in the city's own vineyards

Vienna is a wine city. Vineyards cover the hills of Döbling and Floridsdorf. The city is hedged by 700 hectares of vineyards. It is the only European capital to grow wine within its city limits. The Heuriger is the wine tavern where growers pour their own young wine. The local white to ask for is Gemischter Satz. It is several grape varieties planted together and picked on the same day. At a Heuriger, food comes from a cold buffet counter. You queue, fill a plate with cold cuts and cheese. Only the wine comes to the table. A quarter-litre of young wine at a commercial Heuriger runs €6 to €9. Ride tram 38 to Grinzing or the D to Nussdorf. Then walk uphill away from the touristy core. Cross to Stammersdorf for the local version.

## Eating well without overspending

Beisln serve a soup and main course at midday for about €15. Bakeries offer affordable sandwiches and pastries. A market picnic in a park is a cheap lunch. Tap water is safe to drink across Austria. It is free, so skip the bottled water. Street food is the cheapest hot meal in the city. You can buy a sausage at a stand, a slice of Leberkäse in a roll, or a Bosna with onions and curry powder. Round the bill up by about 5 to 10 per cent. Tell the waiter the total you want to pay. Do not leave the tip on the table.

## Good to know before you go

Austria uses the euro. Cards work in most hotels, restaurants, and shops in Vienna. Smaller cafés, wine taverns, market stalls, and village shops may still prefer cash. Keep some euros for small purchases. US citizens need no visa for stays of up to 90 days in the Schengen Area. Austria is in the Schengen Area. Austria uses Type C and F plugs at 230 volts. US travelers need an adapter. Most shops close on Sundays. Plan groceries and shopping for Saturday. Reserve a popular Beisl for dinner and a Heuriger for groups. The midday menu is the best-value lunch.
